title: Chablis in Depth
description: An in-depth look at Chablis terroir, the four-tier classification, the seven Grands Crus, and how to taste this pure, mineral-driven Chardonnay.

lessons.1.title: The Unique Terroir of Chablis
lessons.1.slides.0.title: The Unique Terroir of Chablis
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Chablis lies at the northern tip of Burgundy, just two hours by car from Paris, yet its terroir is fundamentally different from the Côte d'Or. Here, Chardonnay shows its purest, most mineral face.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: 🗺️ Map of Chablis
lessons.1.slides.2.title: Geography and Climate
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Chablis sits in the Yonne département. The Serein river winds through it, carving an ideal valley landscape. The climate is continental — colder than the Côte d'Or — and spring frost is the greatest threat.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: 📍 Latitude: 47.8 °N — the northernmost point of Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: 🌡️ Mean annual temperature: 10.5 °C (2 °C lower than the Côte de Beaune)
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: ❄️ Frost: April–May is the critical window
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.4: 🔥 Frost defences: heaters and sprinkler systems
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.5: ☀️ Sunshine: long summer days favour ripening
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.6: 🗺️ Distance: 2 hours from Paris, 1.5 hours from Dijon
lessons.1.slides.3.title: The Magic of Kimmeridgian Soil
lessons.1.slides.3.content: What makes Chablis unique is its Kimmeridgian marl, formed during the Jurassic period 150 million years ago and packed with tiny oyster fossils (Exogyra virgula). This soil gives Chablis its distinctive minerality and "gunflint" aromatics.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: 💧 Drainage: excellent — no waterlogging at the roots
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: ⚗️ Minerals: rich in calcium, magnesium and iodine
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.4: 👃 Flavour impact: oyster, shell, chalk, gunflint
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.5: 🌍 Geological era: late Jurassic (150 million years ago)
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.7: 📍 Distribution: the same soil is found in Champagne and southern England
lessons.1.slides.4.title: The Kimmeridgian Ancient Marine Strata, Dissected
lessons.1.slides.4.caption: Chablis stratigraphy: Portlandian above, with the fossil-rich Kimmeridgian below.
lessons.1.slides.5.title: The Magic of Kimmeridgian Soil
lessons.1.slides.5.content: How does this unusual soil shape Chablis flavour?
lessons.1.slides.5.keyPoints.1: • High calcium content: provides the mineral backbone
lessons.1.slides.5.keyPoints.6: • Oyster shell, sea salt, wet stone
lessons.1.slides.5.keyPoints.11: • Higher fossil content → more pronounced minerality
lessons.1.slides.5.keyPoints.12: • Vine roots take up specific minerals
lessons.1.slides.5.keyPoints.13: • The cool climate preserves high acidity
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Chablis vs Côte d'Or Chardonnay
lessons.1.slides.6.content: Same grape variety — so why such different styles?
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.0: 🌡️ Climate: cool continental Chablis vs mild Côte d'Or
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.1: 🪨 Soils: Kimmeridgian marl vs predominantly limestone
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.2: 🍷 Winemaking: little or no oak vs barrel fermentation/ageing
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.3: 👃 Aromatics: lemon, oyster, mineral vs butter, hazelnut, tropical fruit
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.4: 💪 Body: light to medium vs medium to full
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.5: 😋 Palate: high-acid and crisp vs round and rich
lessons.1.slides.6.keyPoints.7: 🍽️ Food: oysters and seafood vs cream-sauced poultry
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 📊 Chablis vs Côte d'Or Chardonnay — Style Comparison
lessons.1.slides.7.content: The same grape, two strikingly different styles shaped by terroir
lessons.1.slides.7.data.datasets.0.label: Chablis
lessons.1.slides.7.data.datasets.1.label: Côte d'Or whites
lessons.1.slides.7.note: Scores 0–10. Chablis is famed for its high acidity and minerality; Côte d'Or whites are rounder, fuller and use more oak.
lessons.1.slides.8.title: The Frost Challenge
lessons.1.slides.8.content: Spring frost is the single biggest natural threat in Chablis — in bad years it can wipe out more than 50% of the crop.
lessons.1.slides.8.keyPoints.2: • Young buds are extremely fragile and easily damaged
lessons.1.slides.8.keyPoints.3: • 2017 and 2018 saw losses of more than 50%
lessons.1.slides.8.keyPoints.7: • Sprinkler systems: ice cocoons protect the buds
lessons.1.slides.8.keyPoints.8: • Wind machines: mix the air layers
lessons.1.slides.8.keyPoints.9: • Smoke screens: form a protective layer
lessons.1.slides.8.keyPoints.14: • Growers invest heavily in frost-fighting equipment
lessons.1.slides.9.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.9.points.0: 🌊 Kimmeridgian is named after the village of Kimmeridge in Dorset, England
lessons.1.slides.9.points.1: 🌊 The same soil also surfaces in Champagne and southern England
lessons.1.slides.9.points.2: 🌊 The higher the fossil content, the more obvious the minerality
lessons.1.slides.9.points.3: 🌊 Frost in 2017 and 2018 cut production by more than 50%
lessons.1.slides.9.points.4: 🌊 Chablis grows only Chardonnay — a single-variety appellation
lessons.1.slides.9.points.5: 🌊 The Serein river moderates the micro-climate and reduces frost risk
lessons.1.slides.10.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.0.question: What is the core character of Chablis?
A. Rich and buttery, with ripe tropical fruit
B. High-acid and mineral, with a distinctive flinty edge
C. Sweet, with a round and luscious palate
D. Low-acid and high-alcohol, very easy-drinking
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.0.explanat: Chablis lies in the northernmost, coolest part of Burgundy. Combined with Kimmeridgian limestone (rich in ancient oyster fossils), Chardonnay here shows high acidity, a lean frame, marked minerality and a distinctive flinty aroma — the polar opposite of the buttery style of the Côte de Beaune to the south.
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.1.question: What makes the Kimmeridgian soil of Chablis so distinctive?
A. Iron-rich, lending red wines their depth of colour
B. Cretaceous limestone, packed with ancient oyster fossils, providing distinctive minerality
C. Volcanic colluvium, lending a smoky, mineral note
D. Sandy gravel, suited to early-ripening varieties
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.1.explanat: Kimmeridgian (Kimméridgien) is a chalky limestone from the late Jurassic period, packed with tiny oyster fossils. It is the most prized soil in Chablis and the geological foundation of its minerality and unique character — found only in the Côte de Nuits and the best Chablis sites.
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.2.question: What is the highest tier of Chablis white wine called?
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.2.explanat: The Chablis AOC system has four tiers: Petit Chablis (entry level) < Chablis < Chablis Premier Cru (17 Premier Cru sites) < Chablis Grand Cru (7 Grand Cru sites such as Blanchot and Les Clos — the very top).
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.3.question: Which of the following are Chablis Grands Crus? (multiple answers)
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.3.explanat: There are 7 Chablis Grands Crus: Les Clos, Blanchot, Valmur, Grenouilles, Bougros, Les Preuses and Vaudésir — all on the same north-Chablis slope. Chambertin is a Pinot Noir Grand Cru in the Côte de Nuits and does not belong to Chablis.
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.4.question: What is the modern mainstream view on oak use in Chablis?
A. All Chablis must be aged in oak
B. Traditionalists use oak, but most modern producers use stainless steel to preserve pure minerality
C. Chablis regulations forbid the use of oak barrels
D. Only Petit Chablis uses stainless steel; all higher tiers use oak
lessons.1.slides.10.questions.4.explanat: Chablis is divided between two camps: traditionalists (e.g. Raveneau, Dauvissat) use older oak barrels for added richness and complexity; modernists (the majority) ferment in stainless steel to preserve pure mineral flavours and high acidity. Both styles have devoted followers.
lessons.1.slides.11.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.11.content: The cool climate and the unique Kimmeridgian soils of Chablis produce the world's purest, most mineral Chardonnay. It is the textbook example of terroir at work — proof that wine is shaped not only by variety and winemaking, but above all by land and climate.
lessons.2.title: The Four-Tier System and the Seven Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.0.title: The Four-Tier System and the Seven Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 20 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Chablis has Burgundy's clearest classification ladder: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru. The seven Grands Crus are among the most precious Chardonnay terroirs in the world.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: 🗺️ Map of the Four Chablis Tiers

lessons.2.slides.1.regions.1.name: Chablis
lessons.2.slides.1.regions.2.name: Premier Cru
lessons.2.slides.1.regions.3.name: Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Petit Chablis
lessons.2.slides.2.content: The entry-level tier, planted on plateaus and flatter ground where the soils contain less Kimmeridgian.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: 📍 Location: plateaus, plains and the edges of the valley
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.4: 🍋 Flavours: green apple, lemon, white flowers
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Chablis
lessons.2.slides.3.content: The heart of the appellation, accounting for 60% of production and embodying the classic Chablis style.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: 📍 Location: gentle slopes with ideal exposure
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.4: 🍋 Flavours: lemon, green apple, chalk, oyster shell
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.7: 🍽️ Food: oysters, white fish, goat cheese
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Chablis Premier Cru
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Forty climats in total, on the best slopes — showing greater complexity and ageing potential.
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.1: 🗺️ Number of climats: 40 (17 on the right bank, 23 on the left)
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.3: 📍 Location: south- and southwest-facing slopes with the best sun exposure
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.5: 🍋 Flavours: candied lemon, white peach, gunflint, sea salt
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.8: 🍽️ Food: lobster, scallops, fish in cream sauces
lessons.2.slides.5.title: Famous Premiers Crus
lessons.2.slides.5.content: Of the 40 Premiers Crus, several stand out from the rest.
lessons.2.slides.5.keyPoints.0: 👑 The five great names of the right bank
lessons.2.slides.5.keyPoints.1: • Montée de Tonnerre (the largest and most famous, 23 ha)
lessons.2.slides.5.keyPoints.7: 🌟 Top names of the left bank
lessons.2.slides.5.keyPoints.13: • Montée de Tonnerre offers the best value
lessons.2.slides.5.keyPoints.14: • The right bank is generally more powerful and mineral
lessons.2.slides.5.keyPoints.15: • The left bank is gentler and more floral
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 📊 Production Share by Tier in Chablis
lessons.2.slides.6.content: An at-a-glance view of how each tier contributes to total Chablis production
lessons.2.slides.6.data.items.0.label: Petit Chablis
lessons.2.slides.6.data.items.1.label: Chablis
lessons.2.slides.6.data.items.2.label: Premier Cru
lessons.2.slides.6.data.items.3.label: Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.6.note: Grand Cru accounts for just 2% of production, yet costs 5–10 times the basic tier. Premier Cru, at 23%, is the sweet spot for quality and price.

lessons.2.slides.7.regions.0.name: Bougros
lessons.2.slides.7.regions.1.name: Preuses
lessons.2.slides.7.regions.2.name: Vaudésir
lessons.2.slides.7.regions.3.name: Grenouilles

lessons.2.slides.7.regions.6.name: Blanchot
lessons.2.slides.8.title: Chablis Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.8.content: Just 100 hectares — seven contiguous vineyards on a single southwest-facing slope on the right bank of the Serein. The summit of Chablis.
lessons.2.slides.8.keyPoints.3: 🪨 Soils: the very finest Kimmeridgian marl
lessons.2.slides.8.keyPoints.4: 📍 Location: a single slope on the right bank of the Serein
lessons.2.slides.8.keyPoints.6: 👃 Style: ultimate complexity, depth and explosive minerality
lessons.2.slides.8.keyPoints.7: 🍋 Flavours: honey, toasted hazelnut, gunflint, wet stone, savoury salinity
lessons.2.slides.8.keyPoints.10: 🍽️ Food: lobster, foie gras, truffle, aged cheeses
lessons.2.slides.9.title: Les Clos: King of the Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.9.content: Les Clos is the largest of the seven Grands Crus (26.9 ha) and widely considered the greatest — the most powerful and the longest-lived.
lessons.2.slides.9.keyPoints.1: 📍 Location: the centre of the slope, the best aspect
lessons.2.slides.9.keyPoints.3: ☀️ Micro-climate: the warmest and most sheltered
lessons.2.slides.10.title: The Three Western Vineyards: The Elegant Camp
lessons.2.slides.10.content: Bougros, Preuses and Vaudésir, on the western half of the slope, show a more elegant and refined style.
lessons.2.slides.10.keyPoints.3: • Style: powerful and mineral, with sea-breeze salinity
lessons.2.slides.10.keyPoints.4: • Signature: the most maritime in feel
lessons.2.slides.10.keyPoints.10: • Signature: the most delicate and graceful
lessons.2.slides.10.keyPoints.11: • Special: includes part of La Moutonne
lessons.2.slides.10.keyPoints.15: • Location: the centre-west of the slope
lessons.2.slides.10.keyPoints.17: • Special: also includes part of La Moutonne
lessons.2.slides.11.title: The Three Central Vineyards: The Powerful Camp
lessons.2.slides.11.content: Grenouilles, Valmur and Les Clos sit at the centre and east of the slope, with greater structural depth.
lessons.2.slides.11.keyPoints.2: • Location: the centre of the slope
lessons.2.slides.11.keyPoints.4: • Signature: the fullest and most supple
lessons.2.slides.11.keyPoints.8: • Location: just east of Les Clos
lessons.2.slides.11.keyPoints.14: • Location: the heart of the slope
lessons.2.slides.11.keyPoints.15: • Style: the most powerful and the deepest
lessons.2.slides.11.keyPoints.16: • Signature: the king of the Grands Crus (covered in detail above)
lessons.2.slides.12.title: Blanchot: The Eastern Jewel
lessons.2.slides.12.content: The easternmost Grand Cru, Blanchot shows a singular light, elegant style.
lessons.2.slides.12.keyPoints.2: 🪨 Soils: a higher proportion of chalk
lessons.2.slides.12.keyPoints.6: • Light and elegant (relative to the other Grands Crus)
lessons.2.slides.12.keyPoints.9: • Lovely young as well as aged
lessons.2.slides.12.keyPoints.12: • The most elegant and refined of the Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.12.keyPoints.13: • Suits drinkers who prefer a lighter style
lessons.2.slides.12.keyPoints.17: 🍷 Best for: those exploring a Grand Cru for the first time
lessons.2.slides.13.title: La Moutonne: The Eighth Grand Cru?
lessons.2.slides.13.content: La Moutonne is the monopole of Domaine Long-Depaquit (part of Albert Bichot), straddling the Preuses and Vaudésir Grands Crus. It is not officially the eighth Grand Cru, but enjoys equal standing.
lessons.2.slides.13.keyPoints.4: ⚖️ Legal status: may be labelled as Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.13.keyPoints.7: • Combines the strengths of both vineyards
lessons.2.slides.13.keyPoints.13: • The only "unofficial" site allowed to bear its own name
lessons.2.slides.13.keyPoints.14: • Long history (established back in the 19th century)
lessons.2.slides.13.keyPoints.15: • Quality on a par with any Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.14.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.14.points.0: 🍾 Grand Cru is just 2% of total Chablis production — extremely rare
lessons.2.slides.14.points.1: 🍾 The seven Grands Crus form one continuous southwest-facing slope — geographically unique
lessons.2.slides.14.points.2: 🍾 Les Clos is widely considered king, but each site has its own personality
lessons.2.slides.14.points.3: 🍾 La Moutonne is not officially the eighth Grand Cru, but its quality is on the same level
lessons.2.slides.14.points.4: 🍾 The Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre rivals Grand Cru quality at much better value
lessons.2.slides.14.points.5: 🍾 The Chablis classification is exceptionally clear — easier to grasp than the Côte d'Or

lessons.3.title: Tasting Chablis and Food Pairing
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Tasting Chablis and Food Pairing
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: The high acidity and minerality of Chablis make it a brilliant food wine, especially with seafood. Knowing the flavour profile of each tier will help you pair it most effectively.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Keys to Tasting Chablis
lessons.3.slides.1.content: To experience the minerality and high acidity of Chablis fully, pay attention to temperature, glassware and tasting technique.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.2: • Aged Grand Cru can go up to 12–14 °C
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.5: • Concentrates the aromatics at the rim
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.9: • Young: pale gold with a green tinge
lessons.3.slides.2.title: Petit Chablis: Flavour Profile
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Entry level — simple, crisp and easy-drinking.
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Chablis: Flavour Profile
lessons.3.slides.3.content: The classic Chablis style, with clear minerality — the most archetypal expression.
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.3: • Minerality starts to come through clearly
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Premier Cru: Flavour Profile
lessons.3.slides.4.content: A clear step up in complexity, with stronger minerality and a clearer expression of terroir.
lessons.3.slides.4.keyPoints.8: • Perfect balance of acidity and fruit
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Grand Cru: Flavour Profile
lessons.3.slides.5.content: Ultimate complexity, perfect balance — Chablis at its peak.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Classic Pairings: Seafood
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Chablis and seafood are a match made in heaven — the minerality echoes the flavours of the sea.
lessons.3.slides.6.keyPoints.6: • Doesn't overwhelm; lifts the natural sweetness of the fish
lessons.3.slides.6.keyPoints.9: 🦞 Roast lobster with cream sauce × Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.6.keyPoints.10: • Enough body and complexity to stand up
lessons.3.slides.6.keyPoints.14: • The pure style doesn't interfere with the delicate fish
lessons.3.slides.6.keyPoints.17: 🦐 Mussels in white wine × Premier Cru
lessons.3.slides.7.title: Classic Pairings: Beyond Seafood
lessons.3.slides.7.content: Chablis goes far beyond seafood — it pairs beautifully with cheese, poultry and fried dishes too.
lessons.3.slides.7.keyPoints.0: 🧀 Goat cheese × Petit Chablis or Chablis
lessons.3.slides.7.keyPoints.2: • Minerality echoes the terroir of the cheese
lessons.3.slides.7.keyPoints.5: 🍗 Roast chicken with creamed mushrooms × Premier Cru (oaked)
lessons.3.slides.7.keyPoints.6: • Subtle oak meets the earthy mushrooms
lessons.3.slides.7.keyPoints.10: • High acidity cuts through the oil
lessons.3.slides.7.keyPoints.18: • Enough body to balance the rich sauce
lessons.3.slides.8.title: Oaked vs Unoaked
lessons.3.slides.8.content: Chablis winemaking is split between two camps: traditionalists stay with stainless steel for purity; modernists use some oak for added complexity.
lessons.3.slides.8.keyPoints.4: • Philosophy: preserve the pure essence of Chardonnay
lessons.3.slides.8.keyPoints.7: • Leading estates: William Fèvre, Droin, Long-Depaquit
lessons.3.slides.8.keyPoints.9: • Food: roast fish, cream sauces, aged cheese
lessons.3.slides.8.keyPoints.10: • Philosophy: build complexity and ageing potential
lessons.3.slides.9.title: Decanting and Service
lessons.3.slides.9.content: Proper decanting and service let Chablis shine.
lessons.3.slides.9.keyPoints.1: • Petit Chablis: no decanting needed — drink as soon as opened
lessons.3.slides.9.keyPoints.3: • Premier Cru: 30 minutes to 1 hour after opening
lessons.3.slides.9.keyPoints.4: • Grand Cru: decant for 30 minutes to 1 hour
lessons.3.slides.9.keyPoints.14: • Flavours peak about an hour after opening
lessons.3.slides.9.keyPoints.16: • Let the wine warm up gradually
lessons.3.slides.10.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.3.slides.10.points.0: 🥂 Chablis flavours peak about an hour after opening
lessons.3.slides.10.points.1: 🥂 Grand Cru can be decanted for 30 minutes to 1 hour
lessons.3.slides.10.points.2: 🥂 Avoid heavy sauces (red-wine reductions, black-pepper sauces)

lessons.3.slides.11.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.0.question: What is the core character of Chablis?
A. Rich and buttery, with ripe tropical fruit
B. High-acid and mineral, with a distinctive flinty edge
C. Sweet, with a round and luscious palate
D. Low-acid and high-alcohol, very easy-drinking
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.0.explanat: Chablis lies in the northernmost, coolest part of Burgundy. Combined with Kimmeridgian limestone (rich in ancient oyster fossils), Chardonnay here shows high acidity, a lean frame, marked minerality and a distinctive flinty aroma — the polar opposite of the buttery style of the Côte de Beaune to the south.
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.1.question: What makes the Kimmeridgian soil of Chablis so distinctive?
A. Iron-rich, lending red wines their depth of colour
B. Cretaceous limestone, packed with ancient oyster fossils, providing distinctive minerality
C. Volcanic colluvium, lending a smoky, mineral note
D. Sandy gravel, suited to early-ripening varieties
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.1.explanat: Kimmeridgian (Kimméridgien) is a chalky limestone from the late Jurassic period, packed with tiny oyster fossils. It is the most prized soil in Chablis and the geological foundation of its minerality and unique character — found only in the Côte de Nuits and the best Chablis sites.
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.2.question: What is the highest tier of Chablis white wine called?
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.2.explanat: The Chablis AOC system has four tiers: Petit Chablis (entry level) < Chablis < Chablis Premier Cru (17 Premier Cru sites) < Chablis Grand Cru (7 Grand Cru sites such as Blanchot and Les Clos — the very top).
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.3.question: Which of the following are Chablis Grands Crus? (multiple answers)
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.3.explanat: There are 7 Chablis Grands Crus: Les Clos, Blanchot, Valmur, Grenouilles, Bougros, Les Preuses and Vaudésir — all on the same north-Chablis slope. Chambertin is a Pinot Noir Grand Cru in the Côte de Nuits and does not belong to Chablis.
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.4.question: What is the modern mainstream view on oak use in Chablis?
A. All Chablis must be aged in oak
B. Traditionalists use oak, but most modern producers use stainless steel to preserve pure minerality
C. Chablis regulations forbid the use of oak barrels
D. Only Petit Chablis uses stainless steel; all higher tiers use oak
lessons.3.slides.11.questions.4.explanat: Chablis is divided between two camps: traditionalists (e.g. Raveneau, Dauvissat) use older oak barrels for added richness and complexity; modernists (the majority) ferment in stainless steel to preserve pure mineral flavours and high acidity. Both styles have devoted followers.
lessons.3.slides.12.title: Summary
lessons.3.slides.12.content: The high acidity and minerality of Chablis make it the ultimate companion to seafood. Each tier brings its own complexity, but all preserve the pure essence of Chardonnay. Knowing the difference between oaked and unoaked styles helps you pick the right wine for the table — whether traditionalist or modernist, Chablis is always a brilliant choice.
